item.title: Street View to Video - Virtual Road Trip Generator 🎬
item.description:
Links

  • GitHub Repo
  • Live Demo

Project Abstract

Ever wanted to take a virtual walk through the streets of Rome, Paris, or Tokyo without leaving your desk? This project does exactly that! Enter a start and end location, and the app creates a smooth video by stitching together Google Street View images along the entire path - like a cinematic road trip generated from Street View data.

Tech Stack

  • Python - Core logic
  • Streamlit - Web UI framework (love how fast you can build things with this!)
  • Google APIs - Geocoding, Directions, Street View Static, and Places API
  • FFmpeg - Video generation and audio mixing
  • MoviePy - Video processing

Features

The app turned out quite feature-rich:

  • 🗺️ Interactive Map Preview - See your route before generating
  • 📍 Place Autocomplete - Smart search powered by Google Places
  • 🧭 Direction Compass - Shows heading direction overlaid on each frame
  • 🎵 Background Music - Add ambient music to your videos
  • 🎚️ Customizable - Adjust FPS, capture interval, FOV, camera pitch
  • 💰 Cost Tracking - Know your API costs upfront (important since Street View API isn’t free!)
  • 📁 Project Gallery - View and manage all your generated videos
  • 🌍 20+ Preset Routes - Famous walking tours worldwide (Times Square to Central Park, Colosseum to Trevi Fountain, etc.)

How it came to be

I was watching some “walking tour” videos on YouTube - you know, those relaxing videos where someone just walks through a city with a camera? They’re oddly satisfying to watch. Then I thought - Google Street View has imagery of almost every street in major cities. What if I could stitch those images together into a video?

The core idea was simple:

  1. Get a route between two points using Google Directions API
  2. Sample points along that route at regular intervals
  3. Fetch Street View images at each point, oriented in the direction of travel
  4. Stitch them into a video

The execution involved some interesting challenges:

  • Calculating heading - Each frame needs to “look” in the right direction. Had to calculate bearing between consecutive points using spherical trigonometry.
  • Smooth transitions - Too few frames = choppy video. Too many = expensive API costs. Found 10-15 meter intervals work well.
  • Street View coverage gaps - Not every location has imagery. Had to handle this gracefully.
  • Cost optimization - Street View API costs $7 per 1000 requests. Added cost estimation before generation so users know what they’re getting into.

Thoughts

The project scratched a creative itch. There’s something magical about virtually “driving” through streets you’ve never visited. I’ve generated videos of routes in cities I’ve always wanted to visit - the walk from Colosseum to Trevi Fountain in Rome, strolling down Las Ramblas in Barcelona, or crossing the East Side Gallery to Alexanderplatz in Berlin.

Some interesting observations:

  • Street View coverage is incredibly comprehensive in touristy areas, but gets sparse quickly in residential zones
  • The video quality is limited to 640x640 (Street View API limit), but it’s good enough for the vibe
  • Adding background music really transforms the experience - a calm ambient track makes it feel like a proper travel video

The Streamlit deployment was smooth. The app runs on Streamlit Cloud with just a Google API key secret. Though videos are temporary there - gotta download them before they disappear!

This was a fun weekend project that actually turned out useful. Sometimes the simple ideas are the best ones. 🙂

item.title: How to add meta tags to a Streamlit app
item.description:
Introduction

  • Streamlit is a cool Python library to build GUIs for python based web-apps
  • It doesn’t support the feature to provide custom meta-tags for the apps you make and instead always have the default streamlit-tags instead
  • The following steps is based on deploying a streamlit app bundled as a docker which you can deploy in your VPS.

Workaround tl;dr

  • Replace the default index file used by streamlit with our custom file containing meta tags of our own

Pre-requisites

  • Ensure docker/docker-compose is installed on your VPS

Steps

  1. Create an index.html in the src directory with similar contents:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <link rel="shortcut icon" href="./favicon.png" />
    <title>Your Site Name</title>
    <script>
      window.prerenderReady = !1;
    </script>
    <!-- changes to be made here -->
    <script defer="defer" src="./static/js/main.dccfd6b5.js"></script>
    <link href="./static/css/main.f4a8738f.css" rel="stylesheet" />
    <!-- changes to be made above this -->
    <meta name="title" content="Custom Title" />
  </head>

  <body>
    <noscript>You need to enable JavaScript to run this app.</noscript>
    <div id="root"></div>
  </body>
</html>

Feel free to add in more meta tags of your choice.

  1. Update your dockerfile to have a line like the following:
FROM python:3.9

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# important line for adding custom metatags
COPY src/index.html /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages/streamlit/static/index.html
# ensure that the above line is present in your dockerfile

COPY . .

CMD ["streamlit", "run", "Home.py", "--server.headless", "true", "--server.fileWatcherType", "none", "--browser.gatherUsageStats=False"]

Basically we’re copying the index file to replace the streamlit default index.html inside the docker container.

  1. Start the container. eg: docker-compose up You’ll notice that what you get is just a white screen in the streamlit app endpoint. This is because the javascript is not loaded yet.
  2. Find the pid of the container(docker ps) and exec into it to run bash
docker exec -it <pid> bash

This basically lets you go inside the running container and inspect it using bash. Replace the PID with the PID of your container

  1. Go to the path /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages/streamlit/static/static/js inside the interactive bash shell inside container. Note that the python3.9 may be different in your case. In that case, just let cd + tab autocomplete the path for you based on the python version you have installed.

  2. Now do an ls like the following:

ls main*.js
  1. Copy the full filename of this file and replace it in the script tag of the index.html file we created earlier.
  2. Restart the container.(rebuild if necessary too).

This should let the javascript load correctly and have your project be loaded fine with custom meta tags.

If you note that somehow css seems to have broken, then just cd to /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages/streamlit/static/static/css inside the container and do an ls like:

ls main.*.css

Once you identify the the main css file, replace main.f4a8738f.css in the index.html file with this one.

Essentially, we’re replacing the basic html file from streamlit with our custom file and then loading the streamlit libraries(js and css) from their path inside the docker container.

Alright, with these steps, you should easily be able to create a streamlit application with custom Meta-tags.

Bonus tip

Maybe you are already aware of this, but to get meta images freely hosted, just paste your images to postimg.cc site. Upload the image and then paste the url to the meta image tag as the following:

<meta property="og:image" content="https://i.postimg.cc/<code>/image.png" />
<meta
  property="twitter:image"
  content="https://i.postimg.cc/<code>/image.png"
/>

Tada✨
